strengths: Compelling and well-motivated paradigm shift: addressing the fundamental limitation of deterministic trajectory regression (mode averaging, failure in non-convex solution spaces) by reformulating planning as continuous-to-discrete probabilistic distribution modeling over an action vocabulary.

Outstanding closed-loop driving performance: VADv2 achieves state-of-the-art results on the CARLA Town05 Long benchmark with a Driving Score of 85.1 using vision-only inputs, noticeably surpassing prior camera-only (e.g., InterFuser at 68.3) and camera+LiDAR approaches (DriveMLM at 76.1).

Effective integration of scene constraints: The conflict loss cleanly incorporates domain knowledge (agent collision and road boundary violations) to regularize the probability distribution over candidate trajectories.

Comprehensive modular ablations: Table 3 clearly highlights the contribution of each component, demonstrating that both the distribution loss and conflict loss, as well as the vectorized scene tokens, contribute significantly to open-loop trajectory accuracy and collision rates.
weaknesses: Mathematical clarity on training targets: Section 3.3 states that KL divergence is used and trajectories close to the ground-truth trajectory are less penalized, but the exact formulation for constructing the target soft distribution $p_{data}$ (e.g., distance metric, temperature, kernel bandwidth) is not formally defined.

Computational complexity and latency analysis: Using $N=4096$ trajectory queries in a cascaded Transformer decoder could incur non-trivial computational and memory overhead. An ablation on vocabulary size $N$, inference latency (FPS), and memory footprint is missing.

Verification of 'without rule-based wrapper' claims: The abstract notes that VADv2 'runs stably in a fully end-to-end manner, even without the rule-based wrapper', yet the main quantitative benchmarks in Table 1 and Table 2 utilize the rule-based wrapper. Presenting quantitative closed-loop numbers without the wrapper would substantially strengthen this claim.

Lack of real-world open-loop evaluation: Unlike its predecessor VAD, which evaluated heavily on the nuScenes dataset, VADv2 only reports closed-loop experiments in CARLA. Including open-loop planning benchmarks on real-world data (e.g., nuScenes) would further solidify its generalization capability.

strengths: Well-motivated formulation: The paper clearly identifies the fundamental flaw of deterministic regression in end-to-end driving planners when dealing with multi-modal and non-convex action distributions. Reformulating planning as predicting an environment-conditioned probability distribution over a discretized trajectory vocabulary is elegant and sound.

Impressive closed-loop performance: VADv2 sets a new state-of-the-art on the CARLA Town05 Long and Short benchmarks, notably surpassing existing multi-modal sensor (camera + LiDAR) methods like DriveMLM and DriveAdapter despite using only camera inputs.

Comprehensive scene tokenization: The architecture cleanly unifies explicit vectorized instance tokens (map, agents, traffic elements) with dense image tokens, enabling rich multi-task supervision while keeping the planning decoder focused.
Informative ablation studies: Tab. 3 demonstrates clear, incremental contributions of each supervision objective (distribution loss, conflict loss) and the individual scene token types.
weaknesses: Missing ablation on vocabulary size and sampling: The action vocabulary size is fixed to N = 4096 via furthest trajectory sampling, but there is no analysis showing how planning quality, coverage, collision rates, or inference speed scale with varying vocabulary sizes (e.g., N = 512, 1024, 2048, 8192).

Evaluation limited strictly to CARLA simulation: While CARLA closed-loop evaluation is standard, prior works (including the original VAD and UniAD) also evaluated open-loop trajectory prediction and planning on real-world datasets like nuScenes. Including real-world benchmarks would significantly strengthen the paper's claims about handling human driving stochasticity.

Discrepancy regarding the rule-based wrapper: The abstract and introduction claim that VADv2 runs stably in a fully end-to-end manner 'even without the rule-based wrapper'. However, Tab. 1 and Tab. 2 evaluate the model with a rule-based wrapper for fair comparison, and no quantitative results are reported for the pure end-to-end setup without the wrapper.

Lack of latency and computational cost analysis: Evaluating and scoring 4,096 high-dimensional action tokens against scene tokens could introduce nontrivial computational overhead. Profiling inference latency (FPS) and memory usage across the pipeline would be valuable for real-time autonomous systems.

strengths: Compelling motivation: The paper clearly identifies the fundamental flaw of deterministic regression in end-to-end planning—specifically, its inability to handle non-convex feasible spaces and multimodal human driving behaviors. Formulating planning as an environment-conditioned distribution over a trajectory vocabulary is conceptually sound and well-motivated.

Strong closed-loop benchmark results: On the standard CARLA Town05 Long and Short benchmarks, VADv2 achieves state-of-the-art performance, obtaining an 85.1 Driving Score on Town05 Long using camera-only input, noticeably outperforming both camera-only methods (e.g., InterFuser at 68.3) and multimodal camera+LiDAR baselines (e.g., DriveMLM at 76.1).

Effective integration of vectorized representations and trajectory field: Discretizing the trajectory space into a rich planning vocabulary (N=4096) via furthest trajectory sampling and projecting them into frequency embeddings allows the transformer architecture to effectively score candidate actions against structured scene tokens (map, agent, traffic elements).

Comprehensive modular ablations: The open-loop ablation studies cleanly demonstrate the utility of each component, particularly showing that both the Distribution Loss and Conflict Loss are crucial for maintaining low collision rates and displacement error.
weaknesses: Evaluation scope is limited to CARLA Town05: The method is only evaluated in the CARLA simulator on Town05. Validation on real-world open-loop benchmarks (such as nuScenes planning metrics) or more recent, challenging closed-loop benchmarks (such as CARLA Leaderboard 2.0 or Longest6) is missing, leaving its real-world generalization unverified.

Overstated novelty regarding probabilistic trajectory evaluation: The paper claims to be 'the first work to use probabilistic modeling to fit the continuous planning action space.' However, discretizing trajectory candidates and scoring them via learned distributions, energy functions, or cost volumes has been explored extensively in prior literature (e.g., MP3, CoverNet-style planners, trajectory evaluation in robotics). The novelty lies more in the specific architectural integration within end-to-end vectorized driving rather than the concept itself.

Ablations rely entirely on open-loop metrics: While closed-loop evaluation is provided for the main comparison, the ablation study (Table 3) is conducted purely open-loop (L2 error and collision rate). Prior work has repeatedly shown that open-loop metrics correlate poorly with closed-loop driving safety, leaving the impact of specific design choices on closed-loop behavior somewhat unverified.

Unclear impact of the rule-based wrapper: The abstract states that the model 'runs stably in a fully end-to-end manner, even without the rule-based wrapper,' yet Section 4.2 clarifies that for benchmark comparison, a rule-based wrapper is adopted over the policy. Quantitative results directly comparing performance with versus without the rule-based wrapper should be explicitly reported.

Missing analysis on vocabulary scaling and inference latency: Evaluating 4,096 trajectory queries via a cascaded transformer decoder could introduce notable computational overhead. The paper lacks runtime/latency measurements and an ablation on vocabulary size N to substantiate real-time deployment feasibility.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental challenge in learning-based autonomous driving: the ambiguity and non-convexity of planning targets under multi-modal human demonstrations, where deterministic regression often collapses into dangerous intermediate averages.

Comprehensive and impressive experimental validation across multiple diverse benchmarks, including CARLA Town05 (Long and Short), Bench2Drive, NAVSIM / NAVSIMv2, and a proprietary 3DGS-based closed-loop simulation benchmark, achieving state-of-the-art results.

Well-designed and technically sound architecture: combining furthest trajectory sampling (FTS) for vocabulary construction, continuous coordinate frequency encodings, transformer cross-attention with multimodal scene tokens, and a conflict-regularized objective.

Thorough ablation studies that systematically investigate vocabulary sampling strategies, vocabulary sizes, demonstration dataset scale, traffic density robustness, and the specific impact of each loss and token component.

Practical inference characteristics: achieves strong closed-loop performance at competitive inference latencies (~125 ms on RTX 4090) without requiring heavy autoregressive or iterative diffusion steps.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is somewhat evolutionary: discretizing continuous trajectory space into anchor vocabularies and scoring/classifying them against scene contexts is an established concept in trajectory forecasting (e.g., CoverNet, Trajeglish) and motion planning.

The empirical distribution target in Eq. (4)–(5) assigns an indicator (one-hot) label to the single closest vocabulary trajectory for each demonstration frame. While effective, this is essentially standard multi-class cross-entropy classification, making the 'probabilistic field' terminology slightly overstated.

Evaluation specifics regarding post-processing: Section 3.4 mentions that top-K proposals can be combined with a rule-based wrapper and optimization post-solver, while Section 4.2 notes following the standard wrapper practice from TransFuser. It would be valuable to clearly isolate the exact delta of the raw end-to-end model vs. the rule-based wrapper across all benchmark tables.

strengths: Clear motivation and sound problem formulation: Directly regressing a single deterministic future trajectory is well-known to suffer from mode collapse or averaging across non-convex action spaces. Formulating planning as learning a distribution over a discrete trajectory vocabulary is a well-motivated approach to capture multimodality and uncertainty.

Extensive and convincing empirical validation: The proposed method is evaluated across multiple leading benchmarks, including CARLA Town05 (Long and Short), Bench2Drive, NAVSIM / NAVSIMv2, and a large-scale photorealistic 3DGS-based benchmark. It consistently outperforms previous camera-based and LiDAR-fusion baselines across closed-loop and open-loop metrics.

Comprehensive ablation studies: The paper systematically validates the core components, including the distribution loss, conflict loss, scene token representations, vocabulary size, data scaling, and performance across varying traffic densities (demonstrating superior robustness compared to deterministic regression).

Effective integration of scene representations: Combining instance-level vectorized representations (agents, map elements, traffic signals) with dense image tokens and using cross-attention allows candidate trajectory tokens to effectively interact with heterogeneous scene context.
weaknesses: Slightly overextended conceptual framing: The paper frames the formulation as modeling a continuous 'probabilistic field' drawing analogies to NeRF. In practice, the method computes Fourier/sinusoidal positional encodings of discrete trajectory waypoints and passes them into a Transformer decoder over a predefined vocabulary of $N=4096$ trajectories. Calling this a continuous probabilistic field is somewhat superficial given that evaluation and normalization occur strictly over the discrete vocabulary.

Scalability to longer planning horizons: While a discrete vocabulary of 4096 trajectories works well for a 3-second (6 waypoint) horizon, the dimensionality and diversity of kinematically feasible trajectories grow exponentially with longer horizons (e.g., 6–10 seconds), which may challenge the vocabulary-based classification strategy.

Ablation on inference post-processing / wrappers: While the paper notes that VADv2 can run without a rule-based infraction wrapper, CARLA benchmark comparisons follow the standard practice of applying a rule-based wrapper. Explicit quantitative comparisons isolating closed-loop performance with and without the rule-based post-solver on CARLA would better clarify the standalone strength of the learned policy.

strengths: Compelling Motivation: Deterministic regression of trajectory waypoints or control signals often fails in multi-modal, non-convex driving scenarios by generating unsafe averaged trajectories. Modeling planning as a distribution over feasible candidate actions directly addresses this fundamental issue.

Comprehensive and Strong Empirical Results: The method is validated across a wide array of recognized benchmarks, including CARLA Town05 (Long and Short), Bench2Drive, NAVSIM/NAVSIMv2, and a 3DGS-based closed-loop simulator. Across these benchmarks, VADv2 achieves state-of-the-art results with substantial margins over previous camera-based and multimodal baselines.

Well-Structured Ablation Studies: The paper presents extensive ablations covering vocabulary size, sampling strategies (k-means, K-disks, furthest trajectory sampling), training dataset scaling, traffic density robustness, and the individual impact of distribution, conflict, and scene token losses.

Effective Integration of Priors: The combination of instance-level scene tokens (maps, agents, traffic elements) and the explicit Conflict Loss effectively penalizes infeasible and safety-critical trajectory candidates during training.
weaknesses: Conceptual Novelty vs. Terminology Overclaiming: Discretizing continuous trajectory space into an anchor/motion primitive vocabulary and training a transformer/MLP to classify or score candidate trajectories is well established in motion forecasting and trajectory planning. Describing this approach as a continuous 'probabilistic field' (drawing loose analogies to NeRF) is somewhat conceptually stretched, as the implementation is essentially coordinate positional encoding followed by transformer cross-attention and cross-entropy over 4,096 discrete trajectory tokens.

Loss Formulation Clarification: While Section 3.3 presents the distribution loss as minimizing KL divergence between the empirical distribution and the model distribution, in practice it reduces to standard categorical cross-entropy where each training frame assigns a hard one-hot label to the single nearest trajectory in the vocabulary. The paper would benefit from presenting this standard classification/imitation learning loss more plainly without over-complication.

Dependence on Inference Post-Processing: Section 3.4 and Section 4.2 note that practical deployment and CARLA benchmark evaluations utilize rule-based wrappers for filtering and PID tracking. A clearer ablation on how much performance depends on the raw policy versus the rule-based safety wrapper would strengthen the transparency of the method's standalone capabilities.

Reproducibility of Proprietary Benchmarks: While the CARLA, Bench2Drive, and NAVSIM results are on public benchmarks, the 2000-hour human driving dataset and the 3DGS-based evaluation environment appear proprietary and non-standard, making independent verification of those specific results difficult.
